rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The celebrated prophets and their achievements narrated up to this point are arranged chronologically.
rows.anchor: Till these verses, celebrated prophets of God and their achievements have been mentioned, and they were mentioned in a chronological sequence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilyās, Lot, and Jonah are briefly introduced in the verses that follow.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, the prophets Ilyās (sws), Lot (sws) and Jonah (sws) are briefly mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilyās is Elijah of the Torah and lived around 789 BC.
rows.anchor: The Prophet Ilyās is called Elijah in the Torah and he lived around 789 BC.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because 6:85 lists Ilyās with Zakariyyā, John the Baptist, and Jonah, Islahi infers that Ilyās shared their attributes.
rows.anchor: In verse 85 of Sūrah An‘ām, his name is mentioned along with Zakariyyā (sws), John the Baptist (sws) and Jonah (sws).

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some identify Ilyās with Idrīs; Islahi rejects the identification because the Qur’ān names Idrīs separately.
rows.anchor: Some people think that Ilyās (sws) is actually Idrīs (sws); however, this view is not correct.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was Abraham’s relative, was trained and instructed by him, and belonged to the same era.
rows.anchor: Lot (sws) is a relative of Abraham (sws) and was trained and instructed by him. Both belong to the same era.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s account is treated in detail in Sūrah Yūnus and Sūrah Anbiyā’.
rows.anchor: Jonah (sws) is mentioned in detail in Sūrah Yūnus and Sūrah Anbiyā’.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah left his people before God’s permission out of zeal for truth and was punished.
rows.anchor: he migrated from his people before he was granted permission by God; at this, he was punished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After returning, Jonah preached to his people and all of them accepted faith.
rows.anchor: After that, he called upon them to embrace faith which all of them did.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These prophets are mentioned for the same purpose as the earlier prophetic accounts.
rows.anchor: The purpose of mentioning these prophets is the same for which prophets prior to them were mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though they lacked the power of Noah, Abraham, and Moses and worked in alien settings, God advanced their work and their preaching and practice endured.
rows.anchor: yet God furthered their work as well and after them their preaching and their practices continued to survive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s placement at the end warns that even truth-motivated haste is not allowed to a prophet.
rows.anchor: hastiness for the cause of disseminating the truth even if it is caused by one’s sense of honour for the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet must persevere patiently; God alone knows when a nation has lost its potential to accept faith.
rows.anchor: It is only God Who knows when a nation has become bereft of the potential to accept faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilyās introduces his rebuke by addressing his audience as wretched.
rows.anchor: Ilyās called to him people thus: “O Wretched people! While leaving aside Allah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi conjectures that Ba‘balak was named after Ba‘l, with bak a shortened form of Bakkah meaning city.
rows.anchor: shortened form of Bakkah which means “city”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilyās rebukes his people for worshipping Ba‘l while abandoning Allah, the best Creator and Lord of them and their forefathers.
rows.anchor: While leaving aside Allah, the Best of Creators Who is your Lord and of your forefathers, you worship Ba‘l.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created them, endowed them with intellectual and emotional abilities, and alone sustains them as Lord of them and their ancestors.
rows.anchor: He created them and blessed them with all abilities of head and heart; it is He alone Who is nourishing them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi asks what role Ba‘l has in creating or nourishing them that would justify worshipping it.
rows.anchor: so what is the reason of leaving him and worshipping Ba‘l? Does he have a role in creating and nourishing them?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilyās’s rejecters will be presented as sinners; God’s chosen worshippers and those who believed in Ilyās escape that fate.
rows.anchor: all of these rejecters will be presented before God as sinners

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain after prophetic accounts contrasts opponents forgotten by posterity with Ilyās’s enduring name and message.
rows.anchor: those who opposed Ilyās (sws) were forgotten by posterity but God made their name and message live on.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural Ilyāsīn refers to Ilyās’s progeny and followers; Arabic plurals can encompass a noun’s components and corollaries.
rows.anchor: In the Arabic language, such plurals refer to all components and corollaries of the noun they signify.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān similarly uses the plural Ṭūrsīnīn for Ṭūr.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has used the plural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet’s blessings and mercy also extend to his true followers.
rows.anchor: the blessings and mercy received by a prophet also extend to his true followers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated reward formula marks God’s established practice of preserving the name of the faithful and virtuous while their opponents are forgotten.
rows.anchor: God makes the name of such people endure who display such faith and virtuosity, and those who oppose such people are forgotten by later generations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was a messenger; God delivered him and his believing relatives, while the rest of his people were destroyed.
rows.anchor: he too was from among the messengers of God; his people also denied him as a result of which the Almighty delivered him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s old wife lacked faith, remained behind with her people, and was destroyed with them.
rows.anchor: his old wife who was among those who were left behind with his nation because she had deprived herself of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kinship with a prophet has no value by itself; faith and righteous deeds are what matter.
rows.anchor: merely being a relative of a prophet is of no avail; what is of avail is faith and righteous deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Quraysh passed Lot’s settlements on their trade journeys morning and evening, they should consider why God’s practice of destroying messenger-deniers would change for them.
rows.anchor: since they continue to pass by the settlements of the people of Lot (sws) day and night in their trade journeys

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar refrain is omitted because its point was self-evident; the setting made a direct warning to Quraysh especially apt.
rows.anchor: since the repetitive verses were self-evident here they were suppressed and an apt admonition was sounded to the addressees of the sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s account is also found in Yūnus, Anbiyā’, and other sūrahs; Islahi says Torah narrators distorted it.
rows.anchor: how the narrators of the Torah have messed up this account.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recovery, God again ordered Jonah to return and preach to his people.
rows.anchor: the Almighty once again asked him to go back to his people and to preach his message to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passengers decided to cast lots to identify the criminal aboard.
rows.anchor: At last, it was decided that lots will be cast to find out who that criminal was.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After swallowing Jonah, the shark spat him out onto a sandy shore.
rows.anchor: The shark spitted him out on a sandy shore.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passengers believed the ship could not escape the storm unless the apparent sinner was cast into the sea.
rows.anchor: sea the ship will not be able to come out of this storm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lots fell on Jonah, who was thrown into the sea.
rows.anchor: The lots fell on Jonah (sws) and he was thrown into the sea.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Probably a shark swallowed Jonah; God saved him when he recognized his folly and glorified God.
rows.anchor: probably a shark swallowed him but God saved him because he realized his folly and extolled the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish spat Jonah onto a sandy shore, where God grew a gourd creeper to shade him while he was weak.
rows.anchor: The shark spitted him out on a sandy shore. There in order to save him from the extreme heat of the sun, the Almighty caused a gourd creeper to grow.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Jonah recovered, all Nineveh accepted faith; the people numbered almost 150,000.
rows.anchor: This time all the inhabitants of Nineveh – numbering almost one hundred and fifty thousand – accepted faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s story is meant to keep the Prophet and his companions from despairing at their people and to urge them to continue preaching.
rows.anchor: so that they do not get disappointed at the attitude of their people and continue with their preaching

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet stands at the frontier between good and evil and cannot leave it without God’s permission, even from a pious motive.
rows.anchor: A prophet is deployed by the Almighty at a frontier where good and evil forces are engaged in a conflict

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets must endure their ordained trials; trying to escape one trial can lead to a greater one.
rows.anchor: trying to save himself from it he ends up facing a greater trial.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nation needs respite until truth is conclusively communicated to it, and only God knows when that point is reached.
rows.anchor: the respite needed by a nation in which the truth is conclusively communicated to it is also essential

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah wrongly judged Nineveh incapable of faith, but later events showed the whole nation had that potential.
rows.anchor: Jonah (sws) out of his own estimation decided that the people of Nineveh will not accept faith even though later events showed that the whole nation had the potential to do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word abaq refers to Jonah’s departure from his people for another destination.
rows.anchor: had left his people for some other destination.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets do not leave from base desire, but their passion for truth can make them exceed limits; God checks such imbalance because they are a barometer of truth.
rows.anchor: so if they show some imbalance in any way even with this pious motive they are checked by the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah felt offended by his people’s indifference and left thinking he should not cast pearls before them.
rows.anchor: he felt offended and left them thinking that why should he cast pearls before such people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mashhūn means a ship laden with goods.
rows.anchor: The word ِونُحْشَم means “ship laden with goods.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression emphasizes Jonah’s disappointment and desire to leave, and that he boarded a ship ready to go without fully reflecting.
rows.anchor: The purpose of using this word is to show that being disappointed from his people he wanted to leave them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passengers may have chosen Jonah to cast lots because they regarded him as especially respectable, making his own selection ironic.
rows.anchor: he would have been regarded as the most respectable and dignified person on the ship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression abaq describes a slave who runs away from a task assigned by his master; Jonah was treated as such and cast into the sea as punishment.
rows.anchor: the expression عبد بقأُ is used for a slave who has run away from a chore assigned to him by his master.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥūt means a large fish, such as a shark or whale, capable of swallowing a human whole.
rows.anchor: The word  وتُح signifies a large fish. A sea has large fish like sharks and whales

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description blameworthy means Jonah deserved the calamity because God deemed him worthy of admonition; though his motive was pious, he acted without permission and was sternly chastised in proportion to his status.
rows.anchor: since he did this without God’s permission he was chastised by God and such accountability is always commensurate to one’s status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tasbīḥ here is Jonah’s confession and plea for forgiveness in the words of 21:87, and it brought his deliverance.
rows.anchor: it refers to chanting of the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As soon as the calamity struck, Jonah understood it as punishment and turned to God wholeheartedly.
rows.anchor: as soon as this calamity struck Jonah (sws) it became evident to him that he had been punished by the Almighty and he turned to God with all his heart.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s prayer is described as the best expression of confessing sin and seeking forgiveness from God.
rows.anchor: These are the best of words which express confession of a sin and seeking of forgiveness from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At God’s command the fish cast Jonah onto dry land; exhausted and weak, he was shaded by a gourd creeper until he recovered.
rows.anchor: at that time he must have been very tired and weak. However, God made a gourd creeper grow above him which protected him on the sea shore from the heat of the sun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once recovered, Jonah was sent back to preach; Nineveh believed, escaped punishment, and enjoyed life for an appointed time.
rows.anchor: This time all of them accepted faith and God delivered them from His punishment and let them enjoy the pleasures of life till an appointed time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle aw can mean bal, “in fact.”
rows.anchor: The word ْوَأُ or) also means ْلَب in fact).

rows.speaker: the Torah
rows.claim: Islahi reports from the Torah that the believers numbered 150,000.
rows.anchor: It is evident from the Torah that those who professed faith were one hundred and fifty thousand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s closing verses return to its opening topic, a ring-shaped pattern found in many sūrahs.
rows.anchor: This sūrah began with a refutation of the divinity of the angels and of the angels having knowledge of the unseen world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening refutes angelic divinity and knowledge of the unseen; the prophetic stories warn Quraysh that all prophets preached the same religion and that deniers are destroyed while God preserves and rewards His messengers and companions.
rows.anchor: those who denied their respective messengers were destroyed. God blessed His messengers and their companions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage first challenges the Quraysh idolaters to provide a logical argument for worshipping angels.
rows.anchor: First, the Idolaters of the Qurasyh are challenged that if they have any logical argument

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing theme is presented in a new style, beginning with a challenge to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: It is this topic which occurs here at the end of the sūrah in a new style. First, the Idolaters of the Qurasyh are challenged

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic mission prospers in this world and is awarded an eternal kingdom in the next.
rows.anchor: Their name and mission prospered and earned respect in this world and in the next one also they will be given an eternal kingdom.

none: Qur’ān text rendered in English translation only; no commentary point appears in this segment.
